findings.headline: Integration Joint Board partnership with health board faces 'significantly challenging' financial sustainability.
findings.detail: Audit work on Scottish Borders Integration Joint Board (IJB)—consolidated into the council's group accounts—identified it does not have a formally documented Chief Finance Officer role, and faces limitations in risk oversight and strategic planning arrangements. More critically, audit concluded: 'Financial sustainability continues to be significantly challenging for the IJB.' This partnership is responsible for health and social care delivery in the council's area, a major budget area subject to political sensitivity.
findings.matters: A lender assessing group finances will be concerned about the viability of entities within the wider group. Poor financial health and limited governance in the IJB could create pressure on the council to provide additional funding or absorb unplanned costs, affecting council finances and reserves.

findings.quote: Financial sustainability continues to be significantly challenging for the IJB. These key messages were reported by the audit team to the IJB Audit Committee in September 2026.

findings.headline: Council has commissioned external lessons-learned review of Hawick Flood Protection Scheme, with reporting due late 2026; £424 million capital plan ahead.
findings.detail: Following challenges encountered delivering the Hawick Flood Protection Scheme in prior years, the council has commissioned Grant Thornton to conduct a lessons-learned review, due late 2026. This is material context for assessing future capital delivery given the council's ambitious capital programme: £424 million investment planned over ten years (2026/27 to 2035/36), including £105 million of borrowing in the next three years, £78.1 million for school estate (Hawick High School expected completion within two years), and £31.9 million for care villages.
findings.matters: A lender will scrutinise the council's track record on capital project delivery and cost control. Prior delays and cost overruns on the flood scheme, coupled with reliance on £220.6 million borrowing to fund the ten-year capital plan, raise questions about delivery risk and affordability if projects continue to face delays or cost escalation.

findings.headline: Council paid off £5 million of stepped loans early as providers sought to increase interest rates; net borrowing increased £50 million despite £95 million in loan repayments.
findings.detail: The council repaid £95 million of loans in 2025/26, comprising £5 million of stepped loans repaid early because providers sought to increase interest rates, and £90 million of PWLB loans from prior years. This was offset by £145 million of new PWLB borrowing, resulting in net borrowing growth of £50 million. All new loans have one- to three-year maturities. Treasury advisers continue recommending short-term borrowing on expectations of falling rates, but the early stepped loan repayment signals rate pressure and highlights refinancing risk.
findings.matters: A lender will assess the council's debt management strategy and exposure to interest rate risk. The stepped loan repayment indicates providers were signalling rate increases; the reliance on rolling short-term debt creates refinancing risk if rate expectations prove incorrect or if capital investment timescales extend.

findings.headline: Material audit adjustments of £9.1 million were required to asset valuations and IFRS 16 accounting, prompting recommendations to strengthen technical accounting controls.
findings.detail: The audit identified and required correction of material misstatements: £5.3 million overstatement from recording a new school asset both as original and componentised entries; £3.1 million from improper deletion of a disposed school asset; £1.3 million reclassification of lease liabilities; and £0.7 million variance in IFRS 16 PPP contract accounting. Although all errors were corrected before sign-off, the audit team issued recommendations to enhance oversight of technical accounting areas and formalize asset register management processes, indicating identified control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Although the audit opinion is unqualified, the scale and pattern of adjustments—particularly in asset valuation and lease accounting—signals control gaps that could result in material errors in future years, especially given the £424 million capital programme and increasing use of lease arrangements.
findings.figures: £9.1m net audit adjustments; £5.3m land and buildings duplication; £3.1m disposal error; £0.7m IFRS 16 variance; five audit adjustments and four disclosure amendments required

findings.headline: Council faces a net budget gap of £46.1 million over the five years to 2030/31, requiring average savings of £9.2 million annually.
findings.detail: The council's five-year revenue plan (2026/27 to 2030/31) identifies £77.1 million in pressures: £39 million from pay awards, £23.8 million from service priorities and policy changes, and £14.1 million from other non-pay pressures. Against planned spending of £2.1 billion, these pressures create a budget gap of £98.1 million. After accounting for expected council tax increases (8.5% in 2026/27, then 5% annually), learning estate funding, and reserve drawdowns, the residual net gap is £46.1 million (2.2% of expected revenue). Closing this will require sustained annual savings averaging £9.2 million.
findings.matters: A lender will assess whether the council has credible plans to close a significant structural gap. The scale and multi-year duration raise questions about whether savings targets are realistic, whether transformation plans will be delivered, and whether additional reserve depletion or external funding may be needed.
findings.figures: £46.1m net budget gap over five years; £77.1m total pressures; £2.1bn planned spend; £9.2m average annual savings; 8.5% council tax increase agreed for 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council identified pressures totalling £77.1 million over the five years... the net budget gap over the same period of £46.1 million (2.2% of expected revenue spend). Savings of an average at £9.2 million will need to be achieved each year.

findings.headline: 54% of the £8.8 million savings delivered in 2025/26 were non-recurring one-off measures, with these rolled forward to burden 2026/27.
findings.detail: Of the £8.8 million savings achieved in 2025/26, only £4.1 million (46%) were recurring permanent savings. The remaining £4.7 million (54%) were non-recurring measures that do not continue into future years. These non-recurring savings have carried forward into 2026/27, where the council must now achieve £12.9 million in savings (including the brought-forward gap). This pattern indicates increasing difficulty in identifying structural service reductions and growing reliance on unsustainable temporary measures.
findings.matters: A lender will interpret this as evidence that the council is struggling to make permanent service cuts or efficiency gains, suggesting that future deficits may recur if funding pressures persist.
findings.figures: £8.8m savings delivered; £4.1m recurring (46%); £4.7m non-recurring (54%); £12.9m savings required 2026/27 including brought-forward non-recurring savings
findings.quote: Of the £8.8 million savings achieved in year, £4.1 million, 46%, was on a recurring basis. The remainder, £4.7 million, 54%, were achieved on a non-recurring basis. Non-recurring savings are one-off savings that apply to one financial year and do not result in ongoing savings in future years.

findings.headline: Usable reserves declined by £8.1 million in the year and now cover only 39% of identified financial risks, down from 61% five years ago.
findings.detail: Usable reserves fell from £52.6 million at 1 April 2025 to £44.5 million at 31 March 2026, including a £4.9 million drawdown to fund the 2025/26 budget. Unallocated earmarked reserves have remained flat at £7.6 million (1.88% of net revenue expenditure), but their risk-coverage capacity has deteriorated sharply. The financial strategy risk register shows these reserves could now address only 39% of identified risks in 2026/27, compared to 61% in 2022/23, reflecting that the cost of risks has grown (e.g. 1% pay increase costs £2 million now versus £1.6 million four years ago) while reserves remained static.
findings.matters: A lender will assess whether the council retains sufficient financial buffer to absorb service pressures or funding shortfalls. The eroding risk coverage ratio signals reduced financial resilience against shocks.
findings.figures: Usable reserves £44.5m (down from £52.6m); General Fund £36.9m (down from £42.9m); unallocated reserves £7.6m at 39% risk coverage (down from 61%); cost of 1% pay increase £2m (up from £1.6m in 2022/23)

findings.paper_title: Item No. 06 (a) - Annual Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: PWLB interest rates rose sharply contrary to the February 2025 forecast of declining rates.
findings.detail: The Treasury Management Strategy approved in February 2025 forecast falling PWLB rates due to expected economic growth concerns and inflation dampening. Instead, rates rose materially, particularly in late March 2026 following the Middle East conflict. The 5-year PWLB rate, forecast at 4.50% by June 2025, ended at 5.28% on 31 March 2026 (78bp higher). The 10-year rate, forecast at 4.80%, closed at 5.72% (92bp higher). Markets at year-end were pricing in rate rises rather than cuts, with inflation expectations revised upward.
findings.matters: Higher borrowing costs undermine the strategy of under-borrowing in expectation of lower future rates; future refinancing and capital programme funding will face significantly higher costs than budgeted, worsening the council's debt position.
findings.figures: 5-year PWLB forecast (Feb 2025): 4.50% by Jun-25; actual 31 Mar 2026: 5.28%; 10-year forecast: 4.80%; actual: 5.72%; Bank Rate fell to 3.75% as forecast but expected to remain at that level

findings.paper_title: Item No. 06 - Covering Report Annual TM Report 25-26
findings.headline: Council increased borrowing in March 2026 specifically to take advantage of lower interest rates
findings.detail: The council made an active borrowing decision in March 2026 to capitalize on lower interest rates, resulting in increased cash holdings held as short-term investments. Investment balances grew from £1m in March 2025 to £17m in March 2026, held with AAA-rated money market funds and major banks.
findings.matters: Active borrowing and timing decisions on debt issuance indicate financial management sophistication and interest-rate risk positioning that lenders assess when evaluating a council's debt strategy.
findings.figures: Investments increased from £1m to £17m; peak cash holdings £70.5m during year
findings.quote: Overall investment balance was higher as we increased borrowing in March 2026 to take advantage of lower interest rates.

findings.paper_title: Item No. 06 - Covering Report Annual TM Report 25-26
findings.headline: Capital expenditure underspent by £16.1m against mid-year budget, reducing borrowing requirement
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure was £82.3m against the mid-year revised budget of £98.4m. The council's report confirms that the lower capital financing requirement at year-end (£537.7m versus mid-year projection of £546.8m) directly resulted from this capital expenditure underspend.
findings.matters: Capital spending variances directly affect a council's financing requirement and borrowing needs, which are key indicators for any lender assessing debt sustainability.
findings.figures: Actual £82.3m vs mid-year budget £98.4m; CFR £537.7m vs mid-year £546.8m
findings.quote: The year-end total CFR decreased in comparison to that projected as a result of the underspend in capital expenditure during the year.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.paper_title: SBC Pension Fund Annual Report 2025-2026 Audited
findings.headline: Unqualified audit opinion with enhanced governance including cyber security and conflicts of interest policies
findings.detail: The fund achieved an unqualified external audit opinion. Governance was strengthened during the year through introduction of a dedicated Cyber Security Policy and approval of updated Conflicts of Interest and Cessation policies. The fund has 17 identified principal risks with none rated red. The fund received external recognition in LGC Investment Awards 2025.
findings.matters: Clean audit and strengthened governance reduce financial, regulatory and reputational risks to the council.
findings.figures: 17 principal risks identified, none red-rated; unqualified audit opinion; governance policies updated and approved
findings.quote: maintaining high standards of stewardship and achieving an unqualified external audit opinion.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.paper_title: SBC Pension Fund Annual Report 2025-2026 Audited
findings.headline: Next triennial valuation expected to show further funding improvement despite 12.6% cumulative pension increases since 2023
findings.detail: Since the 2023 valuation showing 134% funding, cumulative pension increases total 12.6% (April 2024: 6.7%, April 2025: 1.7%, April 2026: 3.8%), increasing liabilities. However, positive investment returns since then mean the 2026 valuation (to be finalized by March 2027) is expected to show improved funding. Initial results expected December 2026.
findings.matters: Further funding improvement would reduce near-term risk of contribution rate increases to the council.
findings.figures: Cumulative pension increases 12.6% since March 2023; 2023 funding level 134%; 2024/25 investment return 2.9%; 2025/26 investment return 5.7%
findings.quote: the positive investment performance achieved since the last valuation means the Fund's funding position is expected to be stronger than at 31 March 2023.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.paper_title: SBC Pension Fund Annual Report 2025-2026 Audited
findings.headline: Active membership fell to 36% of fund from 39% in 2022, with £11m annual cash deficit funded by investment returns
findings.detail: Active members have declined to 4,839 (36% of total) from 39% in 2022, while pensioners increased to 5,487. Pension payments (£39.9m) exceed contributions (£28.9m) by £11m annually, up from £10m prior year. This shortfall is currently funded by investment income. The fund's maturing membership structure creates structural cash flow dependence on market returns.
findings.matters: A maturing fund reliant on investment returns to cover pension payments creates vulnerability to market downturns; any weakening of returns could force contribution increases.
findings.figures: Active members 36% of 13,466 total (down from 39% in 2022); pension payments £39.9m; contributions £28.9m; net annual withdrawal £11m (up from £10m)
findings.quote: The Fund had a net withdrawal of £11m (£10m in 2024/25) during the year which was funded by investment income.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.paper_title: SBC Pension Fund Annual Report 2025-2026 Audited
findings.headline: Fund underperformed benchmark by 5.7% versus 12.2% with major equity manager changes
findings.detail: The fund returned 5.7% against a 12.2% benchmark. Baillie Gifford's UK equity underperformed by 15.1% and global equity by 11.3%. Post year-end, the fund divested the entire Baillie Gifford UK Equity mandate (£39.6m) and largely exited their global equity position. Morgan Stanley global equity (£115m) was also terminated. These changes show active management response to underperformance.
findings.matters: Investment underperformance affects the fund's ability to remain well-funded; management changes to address underperformance reflect governance vigilance and cost control.
findings.figures: 5.7% actual return versus 12.2% benchmark; Baillie Gifford UK underperformance 15.1%, global 11.3%; Baillie Gifford UK Equity termination £39.6m; Morgan Stanley termination ~£115m
findings.quote: Over the 12-month period to 31 March 2026, the UK Equity and Global Equity mandates returned 7.4% and 9.2% but underperformed their objectives by 15.1% and 11.3%, respectively.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.paper_title: SBC Pension Fund Annual Report 2025-2026 Audited
findings.headline: Employer contribution rate cut from 18.5% to 17.0% following strong 134% funding valuation
findings.detail: The 2023 actuarial valuation (completed March 2024) achieved 134% funding, up sharply from 110% in 2020. This enabled the Scottish Borders Council employer pool to reduce the contribution rate from 18.5% to 17.0% for 2024/25 to 2026/27. This represents a material reduction in the council's fixed pension costs.
findings.matters: Reduced employer contributions directly lower the council's annual operating costs and improve budget flexibility.
findings.figures: Contribution rate reduced from 18.5% to 17.0%; funding improved from 110% (2020) to 134% (2023)
findings.quote: The positive result from the triennial valuation enabled the Scottish Borders Council employer pool, which includes Borders College and Live Borders, to reduce the employer contribution rate from 18.5% to 17.0% for the period 2024/25 to 2026/27.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.headline: Pension fund administration and management risk remains above target maturity with outstanding compliance actions due January 2027.
findings.detail: Risk 501 (Failure to Administer and Manage the Fund in line with Requirements) is scored at 8 (Amber) against a target of 4 (Green). Seven of eight internal controls are fully effective; the remaining one is partially effective due to limited Scottish LGPS-specific training availability. Outstanding best practice actions cover scheme administration, information handling and cyber security.
findings.matters: A governance gap in fund administration and operational resilience represents a risk area that a finance director or lender would monitor, though the fund is actively remediating toward target maturity.
findings.figures: Risk score 8 (current) vs target 4 (Green); 7 of 8 internal controls fully effective
findings.quote: A small number of outstanding best practice actions relating to scheme administration, information handling and cyber security remain on track for completion by January 2027.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.headline: Audit Scotland confirms effective pension fund governance and financial sustainability arrangements.
findings.detail: The draft 2025/26 annual audit report explicitly concluded that the Pension Fund has effective and appropriate arrangements in place for financial management, financial sustainability and governance. This provides independent external assurance on governance of a material council liability.
findings.matters: A lender assesses council risk through independent audit findings, particularly on governance and financial sustainability of material balance sheet items like pension liabilities.
findings.figures: 2025/26 audit (draft)
findings.quote: Audit Scotland's Draft Annual Audit Report 2025/26 concluded that the Pension Fund has effective and appropriate arrangements in place for financial management, financial sustainability and governance.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.headline: Multiple governance actions from 2024/25 remain incomplete by 2026/27, including iConnect system implementation and employer covenant review rolled forward two years without delivery.
findings.detail: Critical actions including iConnect cloud system implementation (planned 2024/25, now delayed to April 2027), employer covenant review, and digitalization of historic records remain outstanding. Additionally, business continuity plan, cyber security incident response plan, and data readiness review are not yet completed. The audit specifically flags that actions planned for 2024/25 have still not been completed and recommends reassessing whether repeatedly rolled-forward actions should remain priorities.
findings.matters: Repeated multi-year failure to complete planned governance and system improvement actions suggests either limited execution capacity or weak governance maturity, both concerning for a fund managing £1bn+ of assets.
findings.figures: Actions not completed: 5 major items; Timeline slippage: iConnect rolled from 2024/25 to 2025/26 to 2027; Covenant review rolled forward multiple years without completion
findings.quote: These same actions were planned for 2024/25 and have still not been completed. The Pension Fund should ensure that actions which are rolled forward are reviewed to identify if they should remain a key priority for the following year.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.headline: Pensioner membership is now 113% of active member numbers, up from 91% five years ago, marking an accelerating structural shift in fund demographics.
findings.detail: Active member numbers have grown only 2.9% over five years while pensioner numbers have increased 28.2%. In 2021/22 there were 91 pensioners per 100 active members; by 2025/26 this rose to 113.4. In the latest year alone, pensioner numbers grew by 342 while active members fell by 20, continuing a multi-year trend of pensioner growth outpacing active membership.
findings.matters: Funds where pensioners outnumber contributors face structural pressure on benefit payment sustainability and heightened dependency on volatile investment returns, creating long-term funding risk.
findings.figures: Pensioners now 113.4% of active members (2025/26) vs 91% (2021/22); Pensioner growth +28.2% over five years vs active member growth +2.9%; Year-on-year: pensioners +342, active members -20
findings.quote: Active members have increased by 2.9% over the last five years, with pensioner numbers increasing by 28.2% over the same five-year period. In 2021/22 pensioners were 91% of active members, but now in 2025/26 this has moved to pensioners being 113.4% of active members.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.headline: Pension fund cash flows are deteriorating sharply, with total annual cash flows down 82% to just £1m and benefits exceeding contributions by £11m.
findings.detail: Benefits paid (£36.976m) exceed member and employer contributions (£27.262m) by £9.714m annually. Net member/employer cash outflows have worsened to £11.019m in 2025/26 from £10.096m in 2024/25. Most concerning, total fund cash flows (including investment income) have collapsed to £1.003m in 2025/26 from £5.533m in 2024/25 – an 82% decline. Investment income itself fell from £24.031m to £20.805m.
findings.matters: A pension fund increasingly dependent on investment returns rather than member contributions faces sustainability risk if investment performance remains weak, particularly in a maturing fund.
findings.figures: Member/employer outflow £11.019m (2025/26); Benefits £36.976m vs contributions £27.262m; Investment income £20.805m (down from £24.031m); Total cash flows £1.003m (down 82% from £5.533m)
findings.quote: The cash flow from dealing directly with members and employers contributions continues to be negative, as has been the case over the last number of years. The value of benefits paid out exceeds contributions from active members and employers.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.headline: Pension fund investment returns of 5.7% are the lowest of 11 Scottish local government pension schemes and significantly below the 12.3% benchmark.
findings.detail: The Pension Fund delivered a 5.7% return against a benchmark of 12.3%, a shortfall of 6.6 percentage points. This was the lowest absolute return among all 11 Scottish LGPS funds in 2025/26, where returns ranged from 12.5% to 5.7%. Significant underperformance came from two equity mandates with Baillie Gifford, which the fund decided to disinvest from in June 2026.
findings.matters: Poor investment returns directly threaten a maturing pension fund's ability to meet benefit obligations when member contributions no longer cover benefits paid.
findings.figures: 5.7% return vs 12.3% benchmark; -6.6% underperformance; lowest return of 11 Scottish funds (range 12.5% to 5.7%)
findings.quote: The Pension Fund delivered an absolute return of 5.7% (2.9% in 2024/25) against a benchmark of 12.3% (5.9% in 2024/25) resulting in a relative return of -6.6% (-3.0% in 2024/25). The Pension Fund's absolute return of 5.7% was the lowest absolute return.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.headline: Pension fund structurally in cash deficit, with annual pensions and costs exceeding contributions by £9m.
findings.detail: The fund has been mature since 2013/14 with more pensioners than active members. Over 12 months to June 2026, cash received was £356m against expenditure of £366m, creating a £9m annual shortfall. This is managed through disinvestments and investment returns, but reflects an ongoing structural imbalance where the council's employer contributions and investment income must bridge a widening gap.
findings.matters: A council with a mature pension fund facing structural deficits faces growing pressure to increase employer contributions to maintain solvency, constraining other spending and affecting overall financial resilience.
findings.figures: Cash received £356m, cash expenditure £366m, resulting in £9m outflow over 12 months; cash position £57m at 30 June 2026 with £50m committed to specific investments
findings.quote: The Fund has been a mature fund since 2013/14 with the number of pensioners and their dependants exceeding contributing members. This in turn has resulted in the monthly cash out goings for pension benefits and expenses being higher than the contributions collected from active members.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care staffing pressures (£518k) being offset by temporary income transfer from Older People services
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is facing £518k of staffing cost pressures that are being covered by a temporary transfer of increased income from Older People services. While income is higher than forecast this year, this one-off solution leaves the underlying staffing cost pressure unresolved.
findings.matters: Structural staffing pressures in Adult Services being masked by temporary income transfers indicate ongoing cost pressures that will need to be resolved structurally
findings.figures: £518,000 staffing pressures offset by temporary income transfer
findings.quote: Adult Social Care Temporary 518 Transfer of increased income forecast to Adult Social Care to off-set staffing pressures

findings.headline: Adult Learning Disability services requiring permanent £1,263k budget increase plus £650k transfers from other services
findings.detail: Joint Learning Disability is receiving a permanent £1,263k increase with an additional £650k transferred temporarily from Planning Services (£211k and £439k). This structural demand increase is being partly funded by reducing Planning's base budget, indicating Adult Services demand is significantly outpacing original budget assumptions.
findings.matters: Unexpected demand growth in a statutory Adult Services area signals demographic or legislative pressures that are likely to recur, constraining future budget flexibility
findings.figures: Permanent increase £1,263,000; temporary transfers from Planning £211,000 and £439,000
findings.quote: Joint Learning Disability Permanent 1,263 1,263 Realignment of Adult Services in line with forecast spend during 2026/27

findings.headline: Education Services facing £650k structural pressure funded only by one-off planning income
findings.detail: Education and Children's Services is facing £650k of unbudgeted pressures that are being covered through temporary additional building warrant fee income redirected from Planning Services. Warrant fees are volatile and non-recurring income, leaving education services structurally underfunded if this pattern continues.
findings.matters: Reliance on variable, one-off income sources to cover structural service pressures is unsustainable and indicates the base budget does not match actual service costs
findings.figures: £650,000 education pressures; covered by warrant income temporary
findings.quote: Democratic Services Temporary 51 Additional building warrant fee income used temporarily to address pressures in Democratic Services (£51k) and Education & Children Services (£650k)

findings.headline: Fleet Management Services facing £385k operational income pressure mid-year
findings.detail: Fleet Management has identified an unbudgeted income pressure of £385k that required virement mid-year, indicating operational challenges in the current financial year. The nature of the income shortfall is not specified, but the magnitude suggests material delivery risk in fleet operations.
findings.matters: Unplanned income pressures mid-year may signal service delivery risks or operational cost overruns that could recur and constrain the council's financial flexibility
findings.quote: Fleet Management Services Temporary 385 Income pressure

findings.headline: Council is drawing on reserves (Change Fund) for transformation projects while also accumulating new reserves
findings.detail: The council is drawing down the Change Fund to finance property rationalisation, Building Energy Management Systems, and Live Borders Transformation (Business World system), while simultaneously transferring £924k to a new allocated reserve for EPR scheme. This suggests both capital constraints and uncertainty about future spend.
findings.matters: Reserve management patterns can signal financial stress (drawing down reserves while unable to fund core capital without windfalls) or poor capital planning discipline.
findings.figures: Drawdown of £49k (Duns Library), £330k (BEMS), £21k (Business World), transfer of £924k to EPR reserve
findings.quote: Drawdown from the Change Fund for property rationalisation within the Duns area (£49k), Building Energy Management Systems across the Council property estate (£330k) and Live Borders Transformation for the implementation of Business World (£21k). Transfer available budget to allocated reserve for Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Scheme (£924k).

findings.headline: Fleet Management Services reporting unexplained income shortfall with analysis ongoing
findings.detail: Fleet Management Services is forecasting a £547k income shortfall. Officers are undertaking analysis to understand the drivers, suggesting this is either new or not yet understood. A shortfall in internal income (charges to other council services) may indicate problems elsewhere.
findings.matters: An unexplained variance suggests either poor internal cost allocation discipline or a service utilisation problem that could signal wider operational issues.
findings.figures: £547k income shortfall
findings.quote: A shortfall in income is currently being reported with officers undertaking further analysis to better understand the drivers behind the variance.

findings.headline: Budget balance heavily dependent on one-off EPR scheme windfall (£2.485m) and volatile Planning Services income (£688k)
findings.detail: The council is using £2.485m of a £3.409m windfall from the Extended Producer Responsibility scheme to support the 2026/27 budget, with only £924k reserved. Additionally, Planning Services income from Building Standards (£688k) is flagged as an income stream that 'can fluctuate significantly'. Both support the apparent balance; neither is sustainable.
findings.matters: The council's balanced forecast depends on non-recurring income and volatile fee income rather than permanent structural balance, indicating underlying deficit that will emerge in future years.
findings.figures: EPR scheme £3.409m total, £2.485m used for 2026/27 budget, £688k Planning Services income
findings.quote: Gross up income from Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) scheme of £3.409m. £2.485m was utilised to support the 2026/27 Financial Plan... This position is driven by increased income within Planning Services, particularly Building Standards fee income, although this income stream can fluctuate significantly and will continue to be closely monitored throughout the year.

findings.headline: Council tax collection at risk following pressure experienced in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council notes that there is a risk that collection pressures from 2025/26 may have an ongoing impact on council tax income in 2026/27. This is flagged for continued monitoring but suggests the council experienced collection difficulties last year that may persist.
findings.matters: Council tax is a core revenue stream; any collection risk impacts financial stability and may require reserve draws if not resolved.
findings.figures: No figures given but flagged as ongoing risk
findings.quote: There is a risk that the pressure experienced in 2025/26 may have an ongoing impact and this will be monitored through the remainder of the year.

findings.headline: Scottish Government funding shortfall of £260k for teachers' pay award being covered through virement, not settled
findings.detail: The council has identified a £260k shortfall in Scottish Government funding for the 2026/27 teachers' pay award. This is being addressed through internal transfers from underspends in other services rather than additional SG funding, creating a contingent risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether Scottish Government funding adequacy is settled or contingent on council reserves and service cuts, and whether pay pressures will persist.
findings.figures: £260k shortfall in assumed Scottish Government funding
findings.quote: Shortfall in Scottish Government funding towards 2026/27 teachers pay award addressed through underspends within other services.

findings.headline: Structural funding gap in homelessness support as Housing Benefit subsidy frozen while accommodation costs rise
findings.detail: Housing Benefits faces a £114k pressure because subsidy rates for homeless accommodation are frozen at a historical level while actual accommodation costs (bed and breakfast, hotels) have risen. The council notes a lack of move-on accommodation is forcing reliance on expensive temporary placements. The pressure may exceed budget assumptions.
findings.matters: This reflects a structural mismatch between government subsidy levels and actual costs that the council must absorb, and signals a growing homelessness problem not being adequately funded.
findings.figures: £114k Housing Benefit pressure, but caseload levels higher than previous years
findings.quote: Pressure due to HB subsidy rates for homeless accommodation being frozen at a historical level and the financial gap between the Housing Benefit awards, based on costs of the accommodation, and subsidy levels increasing.

findings.headline: Adult social care redesign risks delivery of care at home hours due to higher provider costs and staff travel time allowance changes
findings.detail: The council is in the middle of a Care at Home Redesign but tendered prices from providers are higher than planned. Additionally, recent changes to travel time allowances for care support workers will reduce internally delivered care hours unless rostering can be made more efficient. The report flags this as a risk requiring mitigation.
findings.matters: This represents a risk that the council will be unable to deliver planned social care hours due to cost inflation and regulatory changes, forcing either service cuts or further budget overruns.
findings.figures: No specific figures but flagged as area requiring closer monitoring
findings.quote: There is a risk that total externally delivered homecare hours will need to be reduced in order to offset increased costs expected within the Care at Home Redesign project as tendered prices from providers are higher than anticipated. Also, recent changes to travel time allowances for care Support Workers will lead to a reduction in the provision of internally delivered care at home hours, unless more efficient rostering of visits can be implemented.

findings.headline: Adult social care facing £690k staffing pressures and learning disability services £2.3m pressure from care package costs
findings.detail: Adult Services is projecting a £419k overspend with significant structural issues: Learning Disability services have a £2.3m pressure from client commitments and 24-hour care packages; Adult Social Care has a £690k pressure from care home staffing costs. These are being partially offset by savings from Older People's services, masking the underlying pressure.
findings.matters: These are not temporary pressures but reflect structural cost increases in commissioned care (higher package costs) and staffing inflation that will persist into future years and are not yet fully resolved.
findings.figures: Learning Disability £2.287m pressure, Adult Social Care £690m staffing pressure, net Adult Services £419k overspend
findings.quote: Significant pressures from client commitments (£931k) and 24-hour care packages (£291k) partially offset by temporary transfer of available budget from other Directorates.

findings.headline: External placement costs for children in social care forecast to overspend by £3.065m with 7 new placements since budget setting
findings.detail: The council budgeted for external placements of out-of-area children but the service is now projecting a £3.065m overspend, with 7 new placements totalling £1.8m added since budget setting. The council anticipates only £600k improvement by year end, leaving £2.5m+ still exposed. The monitoring report flags that further delays in returning children home or new placements could worsen this.
findings.matters: Children's placement costs are the single largest driver of the council's current budget deficit and represent either uncontrollable demand or failure to execute planned placements back, both material risks to financial stability.
findings.figures: £3.065m overspend forecast, 7 new placements totalling £1.8m, only £600k expected improvement by year end
findings.quote: £3.065k current forecast overspend in External placements with anticipated improvement of £600k prior to the year end. There have been 7 new placements since the budget setting totalling £1.8m

findings.headline: Council Tax collection risk: 2025/26 pressure may persist, and self-catering property reclassification has ongoing impact
findings.detail: The council notes that pressure experienced in 2025/26 on Council Tax growth may continue into 2026/27. Additionally, when the budget was set, the impact of self-catering properties transferring back to Non-Domestic Rates was not fully known. This ongoing reclassification may reduce Council Tax base growth.
findings.matters: Council Tax is a core income stream; persistent collection or growth shortfalls erode the financial position and may signal demographic or economic weakness in the area.
findings.figures: Specific impact quantified in Council Tax Reduction Scheme (£0.234m pressure from 200 additional cases vs prior year average)
findings.quote: When the 2026/27 budget was set, the full extent of reduced Council Tax growth in 2025/26 was not known, nor was the impact of a number of self-catering properties transferring back to Non-Domestic Rates. This may have an ongoing impact and will be monitored through the remainder of the year.

findings.headline: Newtown St Boswells Primary School fire damage: costs being estimated, implications to be reported
findings.detail: Damage to the school from fire continues to be assessed, with costs of repair and restoration still being estimated. The council notes that 'costs and implications will be reported to Executive Committee in due course', indicating the exposure is still unknown.
findings.matters: School fire represents a contingent liability of unknown size; even if eventually funded from insurance or capital allocation, uncertainty over timing and amount is a financial risk.
findings.figures: Costs and repair estimates pending
findings.quote: Damage caused by a fire at Newtown St Boswells Primary School continues to be assessed and costs of repair and restoration being estimated, costs and implications will be reported to Executive Committee in due course.

findings.headline: Homelessness demand creating bottleneck: limited movement from temporary to settled housing and low void availability
findings.detail: Safer Communities reports sustained pressure on the housing system with homelessness demand continuing to outstrip provision. The key challenge is 'limited movement from temporary accommodation into settled housing, which has resulted in a significant bottleneck across the homelessness pathway'. Low void properties and high long-term occupancy of temporary accommodation indicate demand exceeds supply.
findings.matters: A bottleneck in the homelessness pathway signals sustained demand that the council cannot meet, increasing the risk of either service pressure, cost escalation, or reputational/governance risk.
findings.figures: No quantified projection at this stage, but described as a 'key challenge' and 'sustained pressure'
findings.quote: Homelessness demand continues to reflect a sustained pressure on the housing system. A key challenge remains the limited movement from temporary accommodation into settled housing, which has resulted in a significant bottleneck across the homelessness pathway.

findings.headline: Housing Benefits subsidy frozen while accommodation costs for homeless have risen; pressure of £114k
findings.detail: Resilient Communities faces a structural funding mismatch: subsidy rates for homeless accommodation remain frozen at historic levels while actual accommodation costs have increased, creating a £114k budget pressure in Housing Benefits. This is not a one-off variance but a structural shortfall that will repeat annually.
findings.matters: A frozen subsidy rate against rising costs is a recurring structural problem that cannot be managed away through efficiency; it signals reliance on either service cuts or reserve funding that will recur next year.
findings.figures: £114k pressure on Housing Benefits subsidy
findings.quote: Within Housing Benefits there is a budget pressure of £114k because subsidy rates for homeless accommodation remain frozen at historic levels while accommodation costs have increased.

findings.headline: 27% of required £12.965m savings still profiled for delivery by 31 March — only 73% delivered permanently by month 3
findings.detail: Of the £12.965m in savings required, £9.429m (73%) have been delivered permanently and £0.589m (4%) temporarily. The remaining £2.947m (23%) are profiled for delivery by year-end. While this represents improvement on prior year (when only Q1 2025/26 had 2.7m of 7.1m delivered permanently), the council states there remains 'a risk' around some brought-forward savings.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that savings will land. Profiled savings (particularly those brought forward from prior years) are less certain than delivered ones, and if 23% fails to materialise, the council would be back to a £3m+ gap.
findings.figures: £12.965m total required, £9.429m (73%) delivered permanently, £0.589m (4%) temporary, £2.947m (23%) profiled to 31 March
findings.quote: An analysis of the delivery of savings as at the end of month 3 is provided in Appendix 2. This analysis shows that at this time £9.429m (73%) of savings have been delivered permanently, £0.589m (4%) have been delivered on a temporary basis through alternative means, and £2.947m (23%) are profiled to be delivered by 31 March 2027.

findings.headline: £0.4m pressure in adult learning disability driven by two transition clients and 11 new care packages
findings.detail: Adult Services is forecasting a £0.419m pressure, largely from learning disability client package costs where two transition clients and 11 new packages of care are generating £1m of pressure. This has been partially offset by temporary budget transfers from other services, masking the underlying structural issue.
findings.matters: Like children's placements, learning disability care packages are demand-determined and difficult to control; the growth in packages and transition clients suggests sustained demographic or service-change pressures.
findings.figures: £0.419m forecast pressure, 2 transition clients, 11 new care packages totalling £1m pressure
findings.quote: The service is projecting a pressure of £0.419m largely attributable to Learning Disability client package costs where two transition clients and eleven new packages of care are contributing to a pressure of £1m.

findings.headline: £2.4m out-of-area placements pressure driven by 7 new high-cost child placements since budget set
findings.detail: Education & Children's Services is forecasting a £2.4m overspend, with the bulk driven by out-of-area placements for children and young people. Seven new placements arranged since the budget analysis cost an additional £1.8m. The service acknowledges the position is 'highly volatile' and will continue to be closely monitored.
findings.matters: Demand-driven pressures on child placements are difficult to control and represent a structural vulnerability; high-cost placements for children with complex needs are unlikely to reduce mid-year and may signal demographic or service-provision challenges.
findings.figures: £2.4m overspend, 7 new placements, additional £1.8m cost
findings.quote: The projected £2.4m overspend in Education and Children's Services relates to a significant pressure in Out of Area Placements for Children and Young People. This reflects ongoing demand and the high-cost nature of placements required to meet assessed need, with 7 new placements arranged since the budget analysis was undertaken costing an additional £1.8m. The position is highly volatile and will continue to be closely monitored

findings.headline: £2.8m unfunded pressure forecast at year-end threatens balanced position
findings.detail: First quarter outturn forecast shows a significant unfunded shortfall of £2.8m, described as representing a 'significant risk to achieving a balanced year-end position for 2026/27'. The council acknowledges this will require continued management action across directorates to contain expenditure and identify income opportunities.
findings.matters: An unfunded pressure of this scale at month 3 indicates the council is unable to absorb demand pressures within existing budgets and will need to find reductions elsewhere or draw on reserves.
findings.figures: £2.8m unfunded pressure at 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Forecasts prepared for the first quarter of 2026/27, based on the position at 30 June 2026, show a projected unfunded pressure of £2.8m at the financial year end. This represents a significant risk to achieving a balanced year-end position for 2026/27 and will require continued management action across Directorates.

findings.headline: Capital programme reprofiled by £13.5m into future years, reducing short-term delivery but shifting cost pressures forward
findings.detail: Major timing movements push spending on Hawick High School (£10.8m) and Borders Innovation Park (£3.5m) into future years. While the council states that Hawick delivery is not affected, this timing movement changes cash flow and may mask underlying delivery or cost risks.
findings.matters: Persistent reprof iling of large capital projects can indicate either prudent cash management or delivery delays masking cost growth. For a lender, it signals potential pressure on future years' borrowing or revenue budgets.
findings.figures: £13.5m net reprofiling from 2026/27 into future years; Hawick High School £10.8m; Borders Innovation Park £3.5m; Plant and Vehicle acceleration £1.5m
findings.quote: This reflects new funding of £4.4m for Flood resilience, Climate emergency, active travel, energy efficiency and road safety work and a net reprofiling of £13.5m from 2026/27 into future years.

findings.headline: Risk of additional asbestos costs on flagship Hawick High School project during final demolition
findings.detail: Hawick High School is one of two major projects financed by the £56.3m capital borrowing. The council explicitly notes that further asbestos pressures may emerge during the final demolition phase, but cannot quantify or budget for them until the demolition is complete and the new school is occupied.
findings.matters: Cost escalation risk on a major project financed by borrowing increases the probability that the council will require additional borrowing or reallocation from other commitments, worsening its debt servicing position.
findings.figures: Hawick High School represents a multi-year project within the £56.3m borrowing requirement for 2026/27
findings.quote: There is a risk that further asbestos related pressures may emerge during the final demolition of Hawick High School but the position cannot be confirmed until the completion and decant to the new school is complete.

findings.headline: Unbudgeted asbestos removal costs leaving £4.7m capital shortfall with no approved funding solution
findings.detail: Asbestos discovered during demolition of Galashiels Academy (£3.590m pressure) and Peebles High School (£2.060m pressure) is driving £2.6m of unbudgeted cost. After applying £0.9m from emergency reserves, the council still faces a £4.7m funding gap with no solution, only a commitment to 'explore funding options' by Q2.
findings.matters: A lender approving £56.3m of borrowing for major projects (Hawick High School and Tweedbank Care Village) needs to know whether cost control is assured. Discovering material unbudgeted costs after approval suggests scope or site risk management issues, and unresolved funding gaps indicate the council may need additional borrowing.
findings.figures: £5.7m total pressures identified; £2.6m asbestos-related; £4.7m unfunded shortfall; total capital outturn £111.3m against budget £120.3m
findings.quote: Further work to be undertaken during quarter 2 to explore funding options for the remaining £4.7m. An update on this will be brought back to a future Executive Committee meeting.

findings.headline: Council borrowing £56.3m to fund 2026/27 capital programme
findings.detail: Capital borrowing of £56.345m (revised budget) represents the largest single funding source for the £111.3m 2026/27 capital programme. Multi-year borrowing continues across the planning horizon, with £46.2m projected for 2027/28.
findings.matters: This scale of borrowing accumulates over time and affects the council's debt servicing costs and prudential borrowing ratios. Material given the council is also facing cost pressures above budget.
findings.figures: 2026/27 capital borrowing £56.345m (revised budget); 2027/28 £46.166m; cumulative to 2035/36 £115.710m

findings.headline: Borders Innovation Park major regeneration phase awaiting business case approval
findings.detail: A timing movement of £3.535m is required from 2026/27 into future years 'to align the budget with the revised delivery profile for Phase 3, pending approval of the business case.' This is a £6.238m project (revised budget) with phases stretching across multiple years.
findings.matters: A major economic regeneration investment project remains unresolved on governance; phase advancement depends on business case approval, suggesting execution risk.
findings.figures: £3.535m timing movement required; revised budget £6.238m; future years budget £6.904m (2027/28) then £104k (2028/29)
findings.quote: A timing movement of £3.535m from 2026/27 into future years is required for Borders Innovation Park to align the budget with the revised delivery profile for Phase 3, pending approval of the business case.

findings.detail: The council seeks approval to reduce the Synthetic Pitch Replacement Fund budget from £2.265m (revised) to £1.344m (projected outturn) to align with available reserve balance. This represents a £921k reduction funded from reserves rather than new resources.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund capital rather than borrowing indicates either constrained borrowing capacity or a policy choice. This reduces flexibility for emergencies.
findings.figures: Synthetic Pitch Replacement Fund reduction of £921k; reserve balance being deployed
findings.quote: Approval is sought to reduce the Synthetic Pitch Replacement Fund budget to align with the available reserve balance.

findings.headline: £5.65m in unresolved capital cost pressures at two secondary schools, including asbestos remediation
findings.detail: Gala Academy and Peebles High School have identified budget pressures of £3.59m and £2.06m respectively for 2026/27. The council states these include £1.616m and £1.019m of asbestos-related expenditure. The narrative notes: 'Funding options are being considered and will be brought forward to a future Executive Committee. It is not anticipated that this will increase the overall capital programme, however, the funding solution is likely to be phased over a number of years.'
findings.matters: Unresolved funding pressures of this size indicate either future borrowing requirements or reallocation from other services. Asbestos discovery suggests unforeseen lifecycle costs.
findings.figures: Gala Academy £3.590m pressure (£1.616m asbestos); Peebles High School £2.060m pressure (£1.019m asbestos); total £5.650m
findings.quote: A 2026/27 budget pressure of £3.590m has been identified and is proposed to be funded through Planned Programming Adjustments. This includes £1.616m of asbestos-related expenditure, with the balance relating to additional project costs within the approved programme.

findings.paper_title: Item No. 10 - Audit Committee - SBC Annual Report 202526 - Covering report
findings.headline: First-year application of new asset valuation standards expected to receive increased external audit scrutiny
findings.detail: The 2025/26 accounting code changed asset valuation requirements from a rolling 5-year programme to mandatory annual indexation on all assets not formally valued. The council explicitly states it expects increased scrutiny from Audit Scotland on the valuation approach and comparison with other Scottish councils, flagging that the external audit process may result in amendments to the draft accounts.
findings.matters: Asset valuations directly affect balance sheet strength and the financial position presented to lenders; first-year application of new standards creates material risk of restatement during external audit

findings.headline: £95m capital investment planned for 2028/29–2034/35 with no project detail or strategic rationale provided
findings.detail: A line item of £95m titled 'New Investment' appears in the outer years of the capital plan (2028/29–2034/35) with no breakdown of projects, services, or timing. Financing is shown as £105.7m borrowing plus other sources across those years. No explanation of what this investment covers or when it will be decided is provided in this monitoring report.
findings.matters: An unallocated capital commitment of this scale creates uncertainty about future borrowing requirements and capital priorities. A lender needs clarity on what major projects are planned, their timing, and their business justification before assessing the council's medium-term debt trajectory.
findings.figures: £95,000k new investment allocation; £105,685k borrowing across 2028/29–2034/35 period

findings.headline: Three major school building projects pushing combined £4.7m of spend into 2026/27 due to delays
findings.detail: Eyemouth Primary is deferring £1,653k because the project went back to consultation. Hawick High School is deferring £1,757k due to delays in early works affecting main works timing. Peebles High School is deferring £1,280m due to handover delays and programme resequencing. The pattern across three of the council's largest capital projects suggests systemic programme delivery challenges.
findings.matters: These three schools represent £139.6m in total project costs. Timing delays cascade through construction programmes, increasing risk of cost inflation; cumulative delays across multiple major projects indicate possible programme management or procurement issues.

findings.quote: Timing movement into 2026/27 of £1,653k due to the project going back to consultation causing delays in forecasted spend. Timing movement to 2026/27 of £1.280m from 2025/26 to reflect a slight delay in handover and a subsequent shift and resequencing of the programme.

findings.headline: Union Chain Bridge project flagged as at risk with outstanding matters requiring management
findings.detail: The project, led by Northumberland County Council, is explicitly described as having outstanding matters and a risk position that requires active management. The council notes it is working to manage and reduce the risk position, with resolution and conclusion expected in 2026/27. The project has accumulated £2,629k in costs.
findings.matters: A major joint-authority capital project is flagged as at risk; unresolved matters and managed risk position suggest potential for delays, cost escalation, or complications in the partnership.

findings.headline: Unallocated reserves of £7.56m cover only 39% of the council's own identified financial risks.
findings.detail: The General Fund unallocated reserve of £7.56m represents only 1.8% of net revenue expenditure. The council's own assessment in its Financial Strategy explicitly states this level is 'sufficient to cover 39% of the financial risks identified in the finance risk register should they be realised'. Identified risks include failure to control budgets, severe weather, economic downturn, contractual claims and unplanned emergencies.
findings.matters: Reserve adequacy is a standard lender credit metric. A council holding reserves that would cover less than half of its own identified risks, particularly when one risk (budget control failure) is already flagged as having partial control effectiveness, leaves limited headroom for adverse scenarios.
findings.figures: Unallocated reserve £7.56m = 1.8% of net revenue expenditure = 39% of identified risks
findings.quote: The 2026/27 Financial Strategy, approved by Council on 19 February 2026, recommends that the unallocated reserve be maintained at £7.56m, equating to 1.8% of net revenue expenditure and being sufficient to cover 39% of the financial risks identified in the finance risk register should they be realised.

findings.headline: £1.2m drawdown from reserves approved in the 2026/27 budget specifically to fund additional support to Live Borders.
findings.detail: The council approved a £1.2m drawdown from the Change Fund as part of the 2026/27 Financial Plan 'to fund additional support to Live Borders'. This planned use of reserves to top up a specific service suggests structural underfunding or an ongoing service challenge that cannot be absorbed within operational budgets.
findings.matters: Repeated use of reserves to fund ongoing service costs suggests either that the service is underfunded relative to demand, or that cost pressures are structural rather than temporary. A lender would want to understand which and whether this will recur.
findings.figures: £1.2m approved drawdown for Q1 2026/27
findings.quote: A drawdown of £1.2m from the Change Fund was approved as part of the 2026/27 Financial Plan to fund additional support to Live Borders and will be actioned during Q1 of 2026/27.

findings.headline: Treasury reserve was halved during the year, from £8.7m to £4.5m, with no explanation for the £4.2m drawdown.
findings.detail: The Treasury reserve, a discretionary contingency fund, decreased from £8.704m at 31 March 2025 to £4.464m at 31 March 2026. This £4.240m drawdown is material but unexplained in the paper, leaving unclear whether this reflects planned deployment of accumulated funds or in-year pressures requiring emergency use of reserves.
findings.matters: Material reductions in discretionary reserves signal either deliberate spending down of accumulated resources or unforeseen pressures. Either way, it reduces financial flexibility available to absorb future shocks.
findings.figures: Treasury reserve £8.704m (March 2025) to £4.464m (March 2026); release of £4.240m
findings.quote: Treasury reserve	8.704	0.000	(4.240)	4.464

findings.headline: Corporate risk on 'Financial Sustainability' remains Amber with internal controls assessed as only partially effective.
findings.detail: The council's Corporate Risk Register maintains an Amber rating on Financial Sustainability as at April 2026. The risk management report explicitly notes the need to 'improve those Internal Controls that are assessed as 'partially effective' and to progress new Internal Controls that have been added to address further challenges in financial planning and budgetary control.' This indicates acknowledged gaps in budget control and financial planning capability.
findings.matters: A lender assesses credit risk through governance and control quality. A council flagging its own partial control effectiveness in financial planning and budgetary control, particularly during a year of 'significant financial challenges', indicates material control weaknesses.

findings.quote: This corporate risk will continue to be reviewed and refined to improve those Internal Controls that are assessed as 'partially effective' and to progress new Internal Controls that have been added to address further challenges in financial planning and budgetary control.

findings.headline: The council is implementing heightened oversight for 2026/27, including monthly Adult Services review meetings chaired by the Chief Executive.
findings.detail: Acknowledging that 'some Council services continue to operate beyond their means', the council has created spend plans, scheduled monthly Adult Services review meetings (chaired by the Chief Executive) to monitor high-risk areas, rolling out finance training, and deploying new financial dashboards. CEO-level escalation of a service review signals serious management concern.
findings.matters: When a council escalates oversight to the CEO level, it signals control concerns beyond normal line management. This is a governance red flag indicating the council recognises a problem it believes requires the most senior attention.

findings.quote: CMT has taken steps to strengthen financial management during 2026/27 recognising that some Council services continue to operate beyond their means. These include: ... Monthly financial review meetings scheduled to be held for Adult Services, chaired by the Chief Executive.

findings.headline: Homelessness and temporary accommodation face sustained cost pressures from rising RSL rents, repair costs, and growing demand, while Housing Benefit subsidy remains static.
findings.detail: The council explicitly describes 'sustained financial pressures' in homelessness services, driven by increased rents charged by Registered Social Landlords, higher repair/maintenance costs, staffing pressures, and growing demand with longer lengths of stay. Housing Benefit subsidy is static. These structural drivers are expected to continue without changes to subsidy or housing supply.
findings.matters: Homelessness pressures are structural, often grow year-on-year, and cannot be easily reversed. They represent an escalating call on council reserves.
findings.figures: No specific overspend quantified; described as sustained pressures
findings.quote: The Council continues to experience sustained financial pressures within homelessness and temporary accommodation services. These pressures are primarily driven by rising costs across the service, including increased rents charged by Registered Social Landlords, higher property repair and maintenance costs, and ongoing staffing pressures, while Housing Benefit subsidy levels have remained largely static.

findings.headline: A £1.002m Council Tax income pressure materialised from the transfer of self-catering accommodation from the Valuation Roll to Non-Domestic Rates—a risk flagged in advance.
findings.detail: Self-catering accommodation properties were transferred from the Valuation Roll (affecting Council Tax) to Non-Domestic Rates, reducing Council Tax income. This was identified as a risk and has now occurred. Combined with lower growth, it created a £1.002m pressure in the funding position.
findings.matters: A lender tracks funding base stability. Valuation Roll transfers that shrink the Council Tax base represent a structural reduction in future income, not a one-off fluctuation.
findings.figures: £1.002m Council Tax pressure
findings.quote: The outturn funding position reflects a reduction in Council Tax income arising from the transfer of self-catering accommodation properties back to the Valuation Roll for Non-Domestic Rates. This issue was previously highlighted as a risk and has now materialised.

findings.headline: The council diverted £1.0m of additional interest income from reserves to the revenue account to help close a £3.8m Q3 overspend forecast.
findings.detail: Interest earned on cash balances normally transfers to the Treasury Reserve to support long-term financial sustainability. In 2025-26, the council applied £1.0m of additional interest to the revenue account instead, as a one-off measure to help bridge a forecast overspend. This is reserve depletion dressed as revenue balance.
findings.matters: Using reserve interest for revenue shows the council's underlying services cannot be funded from baseline income. It weakens the reserve and is not repeatable.
findings.figures: £1.0m additional interest income diverted to revenue
findings.quote: additional interest received on cash balances held by the Council being applied to the revenue account rather than being transferred to the Treasury Reserve (£1.0m)

findings.headline: Children & Families out-of-area placements overspent by £1.028m due to higher placement costs and numbers than budgeted.
findings.detail: Education & Lifelong Learning reported £1.469m overspend, with £1.028m in Children & Families Social Work out-of-area placements. The overspend reflects both higher placement costs and more placements than the council forecast—a demand-led pressure it could not control or fund.
findings.matters: Out-of-area placements are demand-driven, costly, and often grow year-on-year. A lender needs to know if this is a one-off or a pattern.
findings.figures: £1.028m above budget
findings.quote: Children & Families Social Work out-of-area placements continue to present a significant financial challenge, with expenditure £1.028m above budget, reflecting both higher placement costs and number of placements than originally assumed.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care closed £1.958m over budget; the wider £2.599m Adult Services overspend was only closed by negotiating £2.1m additional NHS funding in Q4.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care overspent by £1.958m driven by care homes, homecare, overtime and agency staffing costs—all structural drivers. The total Adult Services overspend (£2.599m) improved from Q3 only because the council negotiated £2.1m extra NHS funding in the final quarter to recognise delayed discharge reductions and inflationary social care pressures. Without this one-off, the underlying overspend would have been £4m+.
findings.matters: A lender funds councils, not care commissioners. Recurrent overspends in demand-driven care services signal a service being delivered above its available budget with no structural fix in place.
findings.figures: £1.958m Adult Social Care overspend; £2.599m Adult Services overspend; £2.1m NHS funding negotiated Q4
findings.quote: Adult Social Care specifically continues to present a significant financial challenge, closing the year £1.958m over budget, driven by overspends in care homes, homecare, overtime and agency staffing.

findings.headline: Only 46% of required £8.9m savings delivered permanently; remaining 54% achieved through temporary measures rolling forward to 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council needed £8.867m in savings. Only £4.123m came from permanent planned reductions; the remaining £4.744m came from temporary alternatives—spend freezes, vacancy delays, deferred projects—that must convert to permanent in 2026/27. This is an improvement on prior years but signals the council cannot identify enough structural savings.
findings.matters: A lender must distinguish between real, sustainable solutions and temporary deferrals masking structural imbalance. 54% temporary status means the council is deferring hard decisions.

These temporary savings will be 'rolled forward' into 2026/27 for delivery on a permanent basis.

findings.headline: Union Chain Bridge project carries outstanding matters into 2026/27 with risk position being managed down
findings.detail: This cross-council project led by Northumberland County Council is not concluding in 2025/26. Officers are explicitly working to 'reduce the risk position' and manage 'outstanding matters', with completion expected in 2026/27. The vague language suggests unresolved issues on a shared project where timing and cost accountability span two authorities.
findings.matters: Cross-authority projects introduce coordination risk and cost-sharing uncertainty; outstanding matters language suggests either cost escalation, timeline slippage, or delivery complexity that could affect the council's capital programme

findings.detail: Enabling works at Tweedbank Care Village completed ahead of schedule, bringing forward £0.9m spend into 2025/26. However, the total project cost for the main works is not yet set; the report states the cost will be 'determined' by the contract due to be signed in early May 2026. A major social care infrastructure project thus carries material cost uncertainty into the council's multi-year capital plan.
findings.matters: Care facility costs can escalate significantly; a council committing to a multi-year care project with uncertain final cost faces budget risk and potential reserve draw-down if overruns occur

findings.headline: Significant additional asbestos removal costs discovered during school demolition but not yet quantified or funded
findings.detail: The new schools programme (Peebles High School, Galashiels Academy, and Hawick High School) has encountered additional costs for asbestos removal during demolition works. These costs are currently being investigated and will be reported in 2026/27, at which point the council acknowledges it will need to identify funding for them. This represents an unfunded cost overrun on a major capital programme.
findings.matters: An unbudgeted cost liability means the council must either increase borrowing, reallocate existing capital funding, or draw on reserves to deliver these projects; a lender needs to know about such contingent costs

findings.paper_title: Item No. 07 - Counter Fraud Controls Assessment 2025-26 - Audit Cttee 9 Feb 2026
findings.headline: Fraud detection capability enhancement deferred to 2026/27 due to resource constraints
findings.detail: The council's planned data analytics strategy to leverage digital tools for fraud detection has been deferred from the 2025/26 financial year to 2026/27 due to resource constraints. This delays the council's ability to deploy continuous fraud detection and audit assurance activities. The deferral is significant given national trends toward high-volume, lower-value frauds, where data analytics is particularly effective for detection.
findings.matters: A year-long delay in deploying fraud detection tools means reduced capacity to identify emerging fraud patterns during 2025/26, particularly concerning as the national fraud landscape has shifted toward high-volume lower-value cases requiring analytical capability.
findings.figures: Nationally, fraud case volumes have almost doubled while individual case values have halved; detected fraud nationally estimated at £265 million in 2024/25
findings.quote: The Internal Audit Strategy 2025-26 includes a data analytics strategy to leverage data analytics and digital tools – due to resources constraints this activity has been deferred to 2026/27.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting restatement increased reported debt by £31.2m
findings.detail: Implementation of IFRS 16 in 2024/25 required PPP leases for 3 High Schools to be revalued, increasing reported external debt by £31.2m. This is a technical accounting adjustment that does not represent new actual borrowing but affects debt ratios and indicators. The lease liabilities are declining (£107.9m in 2025/26 to £86.6m by 2030/31) as leases run off.
findings.matters: A lender examining debt ratios needs to understand that £31.2m of the reported debt increase is accounting technical, not new borrowing. This affects how to interpret trends in gross debt and must not be confused with actual new borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: IFRS 16 revaluation impact: +£31.2m; Finance leases in CFR: £107.9m (2025/26) declining to £86.6m (2030/31)
findings.quote: The implementation of IRFS16 also required the PPP leases for the 3 High Schools to be revalued which has increased reported external debt by £31.2m. These changes are all technical accounting adjustments and do not impact on the cash position of the Council but have caused significant movements in some indicators.

findings.headline: Capital program of £105.9m heavily dependent on grants (39% self-financed, 61% from borrowing/grants)
findings.detail: The £105.9m 2026/27 capital program is funded as follows: £1.9m capital receipts, £2.0m CFCR, £11.2m government general grants, £23.4m other grants/contributions, £1.0m from reserve funds, leaving £64.1m to be met by borrowing. A significant portion depends on continuing grant income which may not be guaranteed.
findings.matters: If grants reduce or are withdrawn, the council would need to either reduce the capital program or increase borrowing further. Grants are not entirely within council control and represent a contingency risk.
findings.figures: Total capital expenditure: £105.9m (2026/27); Funded by: grants/contributions £34.6m, self-generated £7.2m, borrowing £64.1m. Borrowing as % of spend: 61%
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure – per plan: £105.9m (2026/27); Govt. General Capital Grants: £11.2m; Other Grants & Contributions: £23.4m; Net financing need for the year met by borrowing: £64.1m

findings.headline: Under-borrowed position betting on interest rate falls that may not materialise
findings.detail: The council maintains an under-borrowed position of £51.1m in 2026/27 (actual debt £456.5m vs CFR of £597.9m), using cash reserves instead of borrowing. This strategy is justified by an expectation that interest rates will fall. MUFG forecasts Bank Rate declining from 3.75% to 3.25% by Q4 2026, and 5-year PWLB rates from 4.81% to 4.10%. If rates instead rise or stagnate, the council will have deferred borrowing at disadvantageous rates.
findings.matters: This is a directional bet on interest rates. Lenders need to assess whether the council's rate assumptions are realistic and what happens to debt service forecasts if they are wrong. A 1% rise in borrowing costs would add material expense.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing: £51.1m (2026/27), £33.6m (2027/28); Current borrowing rates: 5-year PWLB 4.81%, 10-year 5.39%, 25-year 6.01%; Forecast 5-year PWLB: 4.10% (end Q4 2027)
findings.quote: The strategy for 2026/27 is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels...The Director of Finance will monitor interest rates in financial markets and adopt a pragmatic approach to changing circumstances: if it was felt that there was a significant risk of a sharp FALL in borrowing rates, then borrowing will be postponed where possible.

findings.headline: Debt service costs rising to 10% of revenue stream by 2028/29
findings.detail: Total loan charges increasing from £23.5m (2025/26) to £27.1m (2026/27) and reaching £35.0m by 2030/31. The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream rises from 9.2% to a peak of 10.0% in 2028/29. This is a material increase in the proportion of revenue consumed by debt servicing.
findings.matters: Rising debt service as a percentage of revenue reduces financial flexibility to absorb pressures and constrains the council's ability to invest in services or maintain reserves. At 10%, this is approaching levels that constrain financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Annual borrowing requirement spiking 37% to £64.1m in 2026/27
findings.detail: Net financing need for 2026/27 is £64.1m, up from £46.6m in 2025/26, driven by a large capital program. The Capital Financing Requirement (the underlying need to borrow) reaches £597.9m in 2026/27 and peaks at £618.7m in 2027/28. The council is bringing forward borrowing to fund a concentrated capital spend period.
findings.matters: A sharp year-on-year increase in borrowing requirement concentrates refinancing risk and changes the debt trajectory. Lenders need to understand whether this spike is sustainable or temporary.
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure – per plan: £97.9m (2025/26), £105.9m (2026/27); Net financing need for the year met by borrowing: £46.6m (2025/26), £64.1m (2026/27)

findings.detail: The council has chosen to use £38.5m of cash reserves in lieu of external borrowing, which it describes as prudent given current rates, but explicitly states requires ongoing monitoring if gilt yields remain elevated, suggesting caution about future cash availability.

findings.detail: Introduction of IFRS 16 required the council to remeasure its outstanding liability for the 3 High Schools PPP scheme, resulting in a £31.2m increase recorded on the balance sheet at 31 March 2025. This strategy relies on interest rate reductions to provide cheaper refinancing when loans mature and must be rolled over.

news_drafts.headline: Scottish Borders' loan charges hit 9.1% of revenue budget as debt rises and reserves fall
news_drafts.lead: Scottish Borders Council's cost of servicing its borrowing rose to 9.1 per cent of its annual revenue budget in 2025–26, up from 8.1 per cent the year before. Interest payable increased from £19.7m to £22.4m as external debt grew by £50m to £399m, driven by capital spending financed largely through loans rather than government grant. To offset rising loan charges, the council drew £9m from its general reserves—money set aside as a financial cushion—reducing them from £52.6m to £43.5m. The Audit Committee was told that the council had delivered £8.8m in planned savings to balance its budget, but only 46 per cent were permanent; the remaining 54 per cent were one-off measures that cannot be repeated. The council remains in an under-borrowed position relative to its capital financing requirement, but the trajectory of debt service costs and falling reserves signals tightening financial headroom.

news_drafts.headline: Scottish Borders faces rising debt costs as borrowing jumps 14% and permanent savings fall short
news_drafts.lead: Scottish Borders Council's external debt rose by £50 million to £399 million in 2025-26, a 14.3 per cent increase driven by borrowing to fund capital investment. The council's spending on loan charges rose accordingly, consuming 9.1 per cent of its revenue budget against 8.1 per cent the previous year. Interest payable increased 13.7 per cent to £22.4 million. Yet only 46 per cent of the £8.8 million in planned savings delivered during the year were on a permanent, recurring basis, meaning the council cannot rely on nearly £4.8 million in future budgets. The council funded two-thirds of its £82.3 million capital investment through borrowing, with government grant covering only 13 per cent. Reserves fell by £9 million as the council applied treasury reserves to smooth the impact of loan charges.

news_drafts.headline: Scottish Borders borrows £50m more to fund capital spending as loan charges bite into budget
news_drafts.lead: Scottish Borders Council increased its external debt by £50 million to £399 million in 2025-26 to finance capital investment, driving borrowing from the Public Works Loan Board up from £330 million to £384 million. The council spent £82.3 million on capital projects—roads, buildings, equipment—of which two-thirds was funded by borrowing. Yet the rising debt is straining the revenue budget, the day-to-day spending on services and staff. Interest payments jumped from £19.7 million to £22.4 million, and loan charges consumed 9.1 per cent of the council's net revenue funding, up from 8.1 per cent a year earlier. To manage the pressure, the council drew down £9 million from its general reserves, money set aside as a cushion for the unexpected, to smooth the impact of loan charges. The council remains in an under-borrowed position relative to its long-term capital needs but faces a structural gap between the cost of servicing past borrowing and available resources.
